title: My Lazy Sourdough Schedule (Works With a Full-Time Job)
creator: Margot Bakes at Home
description:
A sourdough schedule for people who leave the house at 8 and get back at 6. Two loaves, minimal hands-on time, no 3am alarms.

Recipe (per loaf):
500g bread flour
375g water
100g active starter
10g salt

Oven: 250C with lid, 230C without

sentences.t: Hi everyone, welcome back to my kitchen.
Today I'm sharing the sourdough schedule I actually use, because I work full time and I refuse to wake up at three in the morning for bread.
Just so you know, part of this video is sponsored by Wayfair.
Okay, so the whole idea is to let the fridge do most of the work.
It starts the night before, around nine p m, when I feed my starter.
This is Gerald, he's four years old, and he's very dramatic.
I'm feeding him one to one to one, starter, flour and water, and he'll be bubbly and doubled by the morning.
Morning, about seven thirty, before I leave for work.
Gerald has doubled, look at all those bubbles, good boy.
I'm mixing the flour and most of the water together, and then the starter, and squishing it all with my hand.
No fancy mixer, just a big bowl and a wet hand.
Then I add the salt with the last splash of water and squish again until it's all absorbed.
Here's the lazy part, I cover the bowl and put it in the fridge, and I go to work.
The cold slows the fermentation way down, so it's fine to sit there all day.
Okay, it's about six fifteen, I'm home, and I'm taking the dough out of the fridge.
It's risen a little, maybe twenty percent, and it feels a lot stronger than this morning.
I'm leaving it on the counter for about two hours to warm up and keep fermenting.
In that time I'll do two sets of stretch and folds, which takes maybe a minute each.
You grab one side, stretch it up, fold it over, turn the bowl, and repeat four times.
That's it, that's all the kneading this bread ever gets.
By about eight fifteen, it's jiggly, it's domed, and there are bubbles on the sides of the bowl.
Now I'm shaping, which I know scares people, but it's honestly fine if it's not perfect.
I tip it out, fold the edges into the middle, flip it, and drag it toward me to build tension on the top.
Into the banneton, seam side up, and a sprinkle of rice flour so it doesn't stick.
And then, you guessed it, back into the fridge overnight.
Next morning, oven on at two fifty with the Dutch oven inside, and I let it heat for a good forty five minutes.
I tip the dough out onto some parchment, score it with a razor, and in it goes, lid on.
Twenty minutes with the lid on, then lid off, down to two thirty, for another twenty five.
And here it is.
Listen to that crust crackle.
The hardest part, I promise, is waiting an hour before you cut it.
Look at that crumb, open, glossy, and it tastes slightly sour in the best way.
So that's the schedule, fifteen minutes of actual work spread over a day and a half.
Let me know if you try it, and tell me your starter's name, I want to know.
